introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Time allowed: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklet are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (One hour, "Answer all Questions"): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (30 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (1 hour): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c)**

State the zeroth and first laws of Thermodynamics. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Zeroth law of thermodynamics.** If two bodies A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other (no net heat flows between them: they are at the same temperature). This law makes the concept of temperature, and thermometers, meaningful.

**First law of thermodynamics.** The heat supplied to a system is equal to the increase in its internal energy plus the work done by the system on its surroundings:
$$Q = \Delta U + W$$
where $Q$ is the heat supplied to the system, $\Delta U$ the increase in its internal energy and $W$ the work done by the system. It expresses the conservation of energy: energy can be transferred as heat or work, but not created or destroyed.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe an experiment to determine the Specific Heat Capacity of copper. Your account should include a diagram, procedure, precautions, observations and a conclusion. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method: electrical heating of a copper block** (the electrical method).

**Diagram (to be drawn by the candidate).** A copper block of known mass $m$, with two holes drilled in it: in one hole a **heater** (immersion heater, e.g. 12 V, 50 W) connected to a **low-voltage supply** in series with an **ammeter** and a **switch**, with a **voltmeter** across the heater; in the other hole a **thermometer** with a drop of oil (to give good thermal contact). The block stands on an insulating base and is wrapped in **lagging** (felt or expanded polystyrene). A stopwatch is used.

**Procedure.**

1. Measure the mass $m$ of the copper block with a balance. Assemble the apparatus as in the diagram.
2. Read the initial temperature $\theta_1$ of the block.
3. Close the switch and start the stopwatch at the same time. Keep the p.d. $V$ and the current $I$ constant (adjust the rheostat if necessary) and record them.
4. After a time $t$ (for example 5 minutes), switch off and note the **highest** temperature $\theta_2$ reached by the block (the thermometer reading continues to rise slightly after switching off, as heat flows from the heater into the block).
5. Repeat with other times, or record $\theta$ every 30 s and plot $\theta$ against $t$.

**Precautions.**

- Lag the block well and start from a temperature slightly **below room temperature**, finishing slightly above it, so that heat gained and heat lost to the surroundings roughly cancel.
- Put oil in the thermometer hole so that the thermometer is in good thermal contact; stir/avoid draughts; read the thermometer at eye level.
- Keep $V$ and $I$ constant; avoid touching the hot block; use the highest temperature after switching off.

**Observations (example of results, for illustration).** Mass $m = 0.500\ \mathrm{kg}$; $V = 12.0\ \mathrm{V}$; $I = 3.00\ \mathrm{A}$; $t = 300\ \mathrm{s}$; $\theta_1 = 20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$; $\theta_2 = 75\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Electrical energy supplied: $VIt = 12.0\times3.00\times300 = 1.08\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$.

**Calculation and conclusion.** Assuming no heat is lost,
$$VIt = mc\,(\theta_2-\theta_1)\quad\Rightarrow\quad c = \frac{VIt}{m(\theta_2-\theta_1)} = \frac{1.08\times10^{4}}{0.500\times55} = 3.9\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$$
The experiment gives a specific heat capacity of copper of about $390\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, in agreement with the accepted value; any difference is explained by heat lost to the surroundings and absorbed by the heater and thermometer. (If $\theta$ is plotted against $t$, $c = \dfrac{VI}{m\times\text{gradient}}$.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 2 shows a ball M of mass $0.800\ \mathrm{kg}$ moving with a velocity of $10.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ that collides head-on with a ball N of mass $0.4\ \mathrm{kg}$ moving with a velocity of $4.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. After the collision, M acquires a velocity of $6.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ while N acquires a velocity of $12.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2019-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_1.png)

(i) Show that the collision obeys the law of conservation of linear momentum.

(ii) Define an elastic collision and determine whether this collision is elastic or inelastic. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
All velocities are in the same direction (to the right, as the arrows in Figure 2 show); take that direction as positive.

**(i) Conservation of linear momentum.**

Momentum before the collision:
$$p_{\text{before}} = m_Mu_M + m_Nu_N = 0.800\times10.0 + 0.4\times4.00 = 8.00 + 1.60 = 9.60\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$$

Momentum after the collision:
$$p_{\text{after}} = m_Mv_M + m_Nv_N = 0.800\times6.00 + 0.4\times12.0 = 4.80 + 4.80 = 9.60\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$$

$p_{\text{before}} = p_{\text{after}}$, so the total linear momentum is conserved: **the collision obeys the law of conservation of linear momentum.**

**(ii) Elastic collision.** An **elastic collision** is a collision in which **the total kinetic energy of the colliding bodies is conserved** (as well as the momentum); equivalently, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation.

Kinetic energy before:
$$E_{k,\text{before}} = \tfrac12(0.800)(10.0)^2 + \tfrac12(0.4)(4.00)^2 = 40.0 + 3.20 = 43.2\ \mathrm{J}$$

Kinetic energy after:
$$E_{k,\text{after}} = \tfrac12(0.800)(6.00)^2 + \tfrac12(0.4)(12.0)^2 = 14.4 + 28.8 = 43.2\ \mathrm{J}$$

The kinetic energy is unchanged, so **the collision is elastic**. (Check: speed of approach $= 10.0 - 4.00 = 6.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; speed of separation $= 12.0 - 6.00 = 6.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
**OR 6 (d), (e) and (f)**

(i) Define photoelectric effect. *[2 marks]*

(ii) State two experimental observations with regards to the photoelectric effect which classical physics could not explain. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The **photoelectric effect** is the emission of electrons from the surface of a metal when electromagnetic radiation (light or ultraviolet) of sufficiently high frequency, at or above the threshold frequency of the metal, falls on it.

**(ii)** Two observations that classical (wave) theory could not explain:

1. **Threshold frequency.** No electrons are emitted if the frequency of the radiation is below a certain value $f_0$ (characteristic of the metal), **however intense the light is and however long it shines**. Classical theory predicts that any frequency should eject electrons if the intensity is large enough or the exposure long enough, because the energy of a wave depends on its intensity.
2. **The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons depends on the frequency, not on the intensity.** Increasing the intensity increases only the **number** of electrons emitted per second (the photocurrent), whereas the maximum kinetic energy increases linearly with the frequency. Classical theory predicts that a more intense wave should give the electrons more energy.

(Another acceptable observation: the emission is **instantaneous** (no measurable time lag, even for very weak light), whereas classical theory predicts a delay while the electrons accumulate enough energy.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe an experiment to determine Planck's constant. Your account should include a diagram, procedure, precautions, observations and a conclusion. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method: stopping potential of a photocell for light of different frequencies** (Einstein's photoelectric equation $eV_s = hf - \phi$).

**Diagram (to be drawn by the candidate).** A **vacuum photocell** (photoelectric tube) whose cathode is illuminated through a window by a bright white-light source followed by a **monochromatic filter** of known wavelength. The cell is in a circuit with a **potential divider** (rheostat) connected to a battery, arranged to give a **reverse p.d.** (anode negative with respect to the cathode); a **voltmeter** across the cell and a sensitive **microammeter** (or galvanometer) in series with it.

**Procedure.**

1. Place a filter of known wavelength $\lambda$ in front of the lamp; calculate its frequency $f = c/\lambda$.
2. Illuminate the cathode and set the p.d. to zero: the microammeter shows a photocurrent.
3. Increase the reverse p.d. with the potential divider until the photocurrent just falls to **zero**; read the **stopping potential** $V_s$ on the voltmeter.
4. Repeat with at least five filters of different wavelengths (different frequencies) and tabulate $f$ and $V_s$.
5. Plot a graph of $V_s$ (vertical axis) against $f$ (horizontal axis).

**Precautions.**

- Perform the experiment in a darkened room so that stray light does not reach the cell, and keep the **intensity constant** (it does not affect $V_s$, but the zero-current point is easier to find).
- Use a **clean photocathode** and approach the zero-current point slowly from above; use a high-resistance voltmeter.
- Use only frequencies above the threshold frequency; read the meters at eye level.

**Observations (illustration).** $V_s$ increases linearly with $f$: for example $f = 5.5\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ gives $V_s = 0.60\ \mathrm{V}$ and $f = 7.5\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ gives $V_s = 1.43\ \mathrm{V}$.

**Conclusion.** From $eV_s = hf - \phi$ we get
$$V_s = \frac{h}{e}\,f - \frac{\phi}{e}$$
a straight line with **gradient $= h/e$** and intercept on the $f$ axis equal to the threshold frequency $f_0$. Hence
$$h = e\times\text{gradient}$$
For the illustrative readings, gradient $= \dfrac{1.43-0.60}{(7.5-5.5)\times10^{14}} = 4.15\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{V\,s}$, so $h = 1.60\times10^{-19}\times4.15\times10^{-15} = 6.6\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, which agrees with the accepted value of Planck's constant.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A certain element has a work function of $1.90\ \mathrm{eV}$. Determine:

(i) its threshold wavelength;

(ii) the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons when the element is illuminated by light of wavelength $4.50\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$; and

(iii) the stopping potential of this element *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Constants used (no data sheet is printed): $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$.

Work function: $\phi = 1.90\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.90\times1.60\times10^{-19} = 3.04\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

**(i) Threshold wavelength.** At threshold the photon energy equals the work function, $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \phi$:
$$\lambda_0 = \frac{hc}{\phi} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{3.04\times10^{-19}} = 6.54\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}\ (654\ \mathrm{nm})$$

**(ii) Maximum kinetic energy.** Photon energy at $4.50\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$:
$$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{4.50\times10^{-7}} = 4.42\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\ (2.76\ \mathrm{eV})$$
$$E_{k,\max} = E - \phi = 4.42\times10^{-19} - 3.04\times10^{-19} = 1.38\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\ (0.86\ \mathrm{eV})$$
(The light is of shorter wavelength than $\lambda_0$, so electrons are emitted.)

**(iii) Stopping potential.** $eV_s = E_{k,\max}$:
$$V_s = \frac{E_{k,\max}}{e} = \frac{1.38\times10^{-19}}{1.60\times10^{-19}} = 0.86\ \mathrm{V}$$
